newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: World rubber pact enters into force for one year.
newsitem.headline: World rubber pact enters into force for one year.

text.p: A long-delayed natural rubber pact, the world's last commodity price stabilisation treaty, finally came into force on Thursday for up to 12 months.
The bulk of exporting and importing countries agreed to a provisional entry-into-force to give China and Italy, which have signed the 1995 accord, time to complete formal ratification.
China, the world's third largest consumer country, told the meeting that its National People's Congress would "expedite" ratification of the International Natural Rubber Agreement.
Italy also pledged to speed parliamentary approval.
P.O. Thomas, speaking for the International Natural Rubber Organisation (INRO) which will administer the agreement, welcomed its entry into force.

"It signifies the continued keen interest and concern that major natural rubber importers and exporters have in the operation of the international rubber pact, whose main objective is stabilisation of prices," he told delegates in Geneva.
"The agreement has undergone many hurdles which were due to unforeseen circumstances," he added.
The accord was adopted in February 1995 but nearly foundered due to a lack of support from consuming countries, which have yet to reach the 80 percent ratification rate for full implementation.
The United States, the largest importer accounting for nearly 29 per cent of consumption, ratified the agreement in December 1996.
As in the previous pacts, natural rubber prices are to be stabilised through a global buffer stock -- although this time importers must share equally in its cost.
The buffer stock of 550,000 tonnes is the sole instrument of market intervention, excluding export quotas or output controls.

Intervention must occur when there are plus and minus 20 percent variations from the reference price. The price is the same as when an old 1987 accord expired on December 28 1995, or 206.68 Malaysian/Singapore cents per kilo.
International pacts on other commodities -- coffee, cocoa and wheat -- used to have price stabilisation mechanisms, but the economic provisions were abandoned in the 1970s and 1980s.
Thomas said an INRO Council meeting was scheduled from March 10 in Kuala Lumpur. Two earlier pacts in 1979 and 1987 had achieved a marked degree of price stability in the market.
"The agreements have both bought and sold natural rubber and thus worked to stabilise prices on both the high and low sides."
Price stability was a key element in enabling producing countries to formulate long-term national development policies.

"Natural rubber price stability is equally important to consumers in the sense they are assured that their planned manufacturing cost will not be drastically undermined by a violent upward swing in the natural rubber prices," Thomas said.
The U.N. Conference on Trade and Development sponsored three rounds of negotiations on the pact.
The latest pact stipulates it can enter into force only once it is ratified by 80 percent of exporting and importing countries. But they may agree a temporary adoption with an average 75 percent.
Some 97.3 per cent of producers have ratified, including the top five: Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Sri Lanka and Nigeria.
Leading importers -- the United States, European Union and Japan -- have ratified, but they represent just 73.4 per cent, not counting Italy whose parliament has yet to ratify formally.
China, which imports 8.8 percent of the world's natural rubber, told the meeting that Beijing intended to ratify.

"China is expediting its procedure of ratification," delegate Lu Ruishu told the talks. Asked whether he expected ratification within 12 months, Lu told Reuters: "Yes, that is likely. I think it will be soon."
